goal.text: beat the broadcaster's projection by at least 3 runs of average miss, on the latest calendar year, which nothing was trained or chosen on.
goal.lead: At 10 overs, the broadcaster shows a projected score. The agent tries to beat it: predict the final total, and miss by 3 runs less on average.

sentences.headline: Here is how well two simple guesses did against the real final totals in past seasons (2005 to 2022, 2,133 innings). This is the bar the agent has to clear.
sentences.gap: The broadcaster's projection misses by 22.5 runs on average, against 23.9 for the average-total guess, which ignores the score at 10 overs. Knowing the score at 10 overs is worth 1.4 runs (5.9%), and 0.4 more innings in every 100 land within 10 runs.
sentences.finding: The broadcaster's projection is only slightly better than knowing nothing: its average miss is just 1.4 runs (5.9%) lower, so beating it means little.
sentences.bias: The broadcaster's projection guesses 14.3 runs too low on average, because sides tend to score faster in the last 10 overs than their run rate at the halfway mark.

meter.caption: Average miss, runs · 2005 to 2022, 2,133 innings
meter.text: Average miss, lower is better: the average-total guess 23.9, the broadcaster's projection 22.5, the goal 19.5 or less.

hero.caption: A real innings: Australia v India, Sydney Cricket Ground, December 2020. The first 10 overs, in grey, are context; the white part is what everyone is trying to predict. Australia went from 82/2 to 186. The broadcaster's straight line said 164 and was 22 runs short: about its typical miss. Open circles mark wickets.
hero.panel: Knowing the score at 10 overs barely helps the broadcaster, and on average it guesses too low, by 14.3 runs. The agent has to beat it by at least 3 runs.
hero.footnote: 2,133 past innings, 2005 to 2022: IPL, BBL and full-member internationals.
hero.chart_text: Runs by over for Australia v India, Sydney Cricket Ground, December 2020. The first 10 overs are shown in grey as context and the last 10 in the prediction area. Australia were 82 for 2 after 10 overs. The broadcaster's projection said 164. The average-total guess said 162. The innings finished on 186. A zoom on the finish shows where each prediction landed at 20 overs: the actual total 186, the broadcaster's projection 164 (22 runs short) and the average-total guess 162. The broadcaster's usual miss is 22.5 runs either way, shown as a band around its projection. The agent's prediction is not known.

terms.meaning: The program in which a language model chooses ideas and code checks every number.
Plain code, no AI: it tries every combination of settings and builds the best clues for each.
The broadcaster's forecast: the runs per over so far, times 20.
Always guess the typical final total, whatever the score at 10 overs.
One try: a set of clues together with settings.
The facts about an innings a model may use, such as wickets at 10 overs.
Choices made before learning starts, such as how many seasons to learn from.
Seasons used again and again to choose between ideas.
The one season kept sealed until the end, then scored once.

terms.technical: the model chosen on the check seasons
terms.meaning: The idea that scored best on the check seasons.

definitions.brute_force: The brute-force search is plain code, no AI: it tries every combination of settings and, inside each, adds clues one at a time, keeping whichever cuts the miss most. It is the yardstick: if the agent can't match it, its reasoning isn't adding anything.
definitions.brute_force_technical: Technically it is a grid search over 24 combinations of three hyperparameters (which innings, how many seasons, how much recent seasons count), with greedy forward selection of features in each cell.
definitions.brute_force_honest: "Brute-force" refers to the settings only: it does not try every possible set of clues (2^19, about 524,000).
